Frequently asked questions:
Q: Is this consulting or software?
A: Both, by design. You get a platform that maps your organisation continuously, and a team that interprets it with you and builds the automations.
Q: Do we need to change our systems?
A: No. Mission Control connects to the tools you already use. Nothing is replaced.
Q: Can we start with one team or workflow?
A: Yes. Many organisations start with one area where the pain is clearest, then expand once the map proves its value.
Q: How are automations priced?
A: Each one is scoped and priced on its own, after you have seen and approved its business case.
Q: How do we explain this to our staff?
A: We give you a briefing plan and materials. Mission Control measures how work moves, not individual performance, and we recommend saying so plainly.

Frequently asked questions:
Q: Do you read emails or documents?
A: No. Mission Control records when work moves and where it goes. It does not capture what emails, messages or documents say.
Q: Is this employee monitoring?
A: It measures how work flows between teams and systems, not individual performance. We help you notify staff in writing before switch-on.
Q: Can we limit what is in scope?
A: Yes. You choose which teams and systems are included, and can change that at any time.
Q: What documentation can you provide?
A: Architecture, data flow and data handling documentation is available on request for your security review.
Q: Do you hold certifications?
A: We will publish certifications and attestations here as we obtain them. Ask us about current status in your briefing.

## Work about work is a hand-off problem, not a people problem
URL: https://missioncntrl.io/news/work-about-work-is-a-handoff-problem
Published: 2026-11-22

Key points
Large surveys put "work about work" at roughly 55 to 60 per cent of a knowledge worker's week. The figure has barely moved in years, despite more collaboration software than ever.
Most of that time is spent at the hand-offs between people and teams: chasing status, searching for what the last person did, and re-explaining context.
Asking people to focus harder does not fix a design problem. Making the state of each piece of work visible at the hand-off does.
Do not ask people where their time goes. Measure where the work waits, using the timestamps your systems already record.
Every few years another study confirms what operators already feel: most of the working week is not spent doing the work. Asana's Anatomy of Work Index 2022 surveyed 10,624 knowledge workers across Australia, France, Germany, Japan, Singapore, the UK and the US. It found that employees at medium and large companies spend 59 per cent of their day on what it calls work about work. The 2021 Australia and New Zealand cut put the local figure at 58 per cent. The UK figure was 61 per cent.
Microsoft reached a similar conclusion from a different direction. Its 2023 Work Trend Index analysed signals from Microsoft 365. It found the average person spends 57 per cent of their time in that software communicating (meetings, chat and email) and 43 per cent creating. In the same report, 68 per cent of people said they lack enough uninterrupted focus time.
The usual response is a new tool, a no-meeting day or a focus campaign. We think that misreads the problem. Work about work is mostly not a personal productivity failure. It is what an organisation pays for hand-offs nobody designed.
What the surveys are really measuring
Look at what falls under "work about work": status updates, searching for information, switching between apps, chasing approvals, duplicated effort. Almost none of it happens inside one person's task. It happens at the moments work changes hands.
The McKinsey Global Institute's 2012 analysis estimated that the average interaction worker spends 28 per cent of the week managing email. It put nearly 20 per cent on looking for internal information or tracking down colleagues who can help. That second number describes a hand-off failure. Someone needed what a previous step produced, and could not find it or the person who held it.
Research on attention points the same way. Gloria Mark and colleagues at the University of California, Irvine shadowed 36 knowledge workers , timing every event to the second. On average people juggled 12.2 separate "working spheres" a day. They switched between them roughly every ten and a half minutes. Much of that switching is driven by other people's dependencies arriving unannounced.
Treat these figures with care. They come from self-reported surveys, vendor telemetry and older estimates, and they do not agree on method. What matters is that every method lands in the same place: well over half the week goes on coordination. That consistency is the finding.
Why the hand-off is where time disappears
Think about a typical services workflow: a new client is onboarded, an engagement is scoped, a matter is opened, a claim is assessed. On paper it is five or six steps. In practice each step ends with a hand-off. And each hand-off has three hidden costs.
Waiting. The work sits in someone's queue, or in an inbox, until they notice it. Nobody is doing anything wrong. The work is simply idle.
Re-establishing context. The next person has to work out what was done, what is missing and what the client asked for. Some of that is searching. Some of it is a message back to the person who just handed it over.
Status chasing. Because nobody can see where the work is, managers and clients ask. Each question interrupts someone who is in the middle of something else.
None of these show up as "work" in a timesheet. All of them show up as elapsed time for the client and as fatigue for the team. And they multiply with every hand-off. A process that touches seven people has six seams, each leaking a little time.
Why the usual fixes underdeliver
More collaboration tools. Most organisations already have too many places where status can live: email, chat, a practice management system, a CRM, a spreadsheet someone built in 2019. Another channel adds one more place to look. The problem was never a lack of ways to talk. It was that the state of the work was not recorded where the next person would find it.
Focus campaigns. Protecting deep work is good for individuals. But if a case cannot move until three people have each looked at it, protecting their focus time can make the case slower. Reducing interruptions only helps when you also reduce the reasons for them.
Asking people where their time goes. Time surveys and workshops tell you what people remember and what they think matters. They are poor at recovering wait time, which by definition nobody experiences as work. A step that "takes ten minutes" can routinely sit for three days before anyone starts it.
A better approach: measure the hand-offs
The practical alternative is to study the work item instead of the worker. Pick one workflow that matters commercially. Then trace individual cases through it using the timestamps your systems already record. This is the core idea behind process mining , a field built on event logs. Each event carries a case identifier, an activity and a timestamp.
For a first pass, four measures do most of the work:
Hand-offs per case. How many times does a typical case change hands, and how much does that vary? Outliers usually point to unclear ownership.
Wait time per hand-off. How long does work sit between one person finishing and the next starting? This is usually where most of the elapsed time is.
Rework loops. How often does a case go backwards to a step it has already passed? Each loop is a hand-off that failed to carry enough context.
Path variety. How many different routes do cases take in practice, compared with the one route in the procedure manual?
You need a few hundred cases at most to see the pattern. You do not need to watch anyone's screen. Timestamps on records, status changes and assignments are enough to show where work waits. (We cover how to do this without monitoring individuals in a separate piece .)
What to do with what you find
Once hand-offs are visible, the fixes tend to be unglamorous and effective:
Remove a hand-off entirely where two steps can be done by one role. This is usually the cheapest improvement available.
Standardise what travels with the work so the next person starts with context rather than a question. A short, required set of fields at each hand-off often beats a long procedure document.
Make the state of each case visible to the people who chase it, so status questions stop being asked.
Automate the transfer, not just the task. The most valuable automations often move information between systems at a hand-off, rather than speeding up a step that was never the delay.
The mistake is to treat work about work as an individual habit to be coached away. It is a property of how the organisation passes work around. That makes it measurable, and fixable, by the people accountable for how the business runs.
Questions
What is "work about work"?
It is time spent coordinating work rather than doing it: status updates, searching for information, switching between tools, chasing approvals and duplicating effort. Asana's Anatomy of Work research popularised the term. Its 2022 survey found that employees at medium and large companies spend 59 per cent of their day on it.
Why is work about work so hard to reduce?
Because most of it happens at the hand-offs between people and teams, not inside any one person's task. Individual productivity tactics do not change how work is passed between roles. Changing hand-offs requires seeing them, and most organisations have no measure of them.
How do you measure hand-offs without surveying staff?
Use the timestamps that business systems already record when a case is created, assigned, updated or closed. Tracing a few hundred cases shows how many hand-offs each case has, how long work waits between them and how often it loops back.
Sources

Asana, Anatomy of Work Index 2021: Australia and New Zealand findings
Asana, Anatomy of Work Index 2021: UK findings
Microsoft, 2023 Work Trend Index: Will AI fix work?

## Flow efficiency: the number that explains why simple work takes weeks
URL: https://missioncntrl.io/news/flow-efficiency-services-firms
Published: 2026-11-22

Key points
Flow efficiency is the share of a case's elapsed time spent actively working on it. The rest is waiting.
Practitioners commonly report figures in the 5 to 15 per cent range for knowledge work. No rigorous benchmark exists, but even generous estimates leave most elapsed time as waiting.
Little's Law shows why: with demand held steady, the average time a case takes rises in direct proportion to how much work is open at once.
High utilisation targets make waiting worse, not better. Queues grow sharply as people approach full capacity.
The fastest way to deliver sooner is usually to cut waiting, not to make people work faster.
Ask a team how long it takes to onboard a client and you will usually get two answers. The work takes a few hours. The onboarding takes two weeks. The gap between those numbers is where most services businesses quietly lose speed, margin and client goodwill. It has a name: flow efficiency.
What flow efficiency is
Flow efficiency is a simple ratio. Divide the time someone spent actively working on a case by the total elapsed time from start to finish:
Flow efficiency = active time ÷ total elapsed time
A matter that receives six hours of actual work across ten working days (80 working hours) has a flow efficiency of 7.5 per cent. For the other 92.5 per cent of the time it was waiting.
The idea comes from lean operations. It was popularised for knowledge work by Niklas Modig and Pär Åhlström, who contrast resource efficiency (keeping people busy) with flow efficiency (keeping work moving). One practitioner summary puts the shift well: watch the ball, not the player. In knowledge work what matters most is what is happening to the work, not what the workers are doing.
How low is it, really?
Figures in the 5 to 15 per cent range are widely quoted. ASOS's engineering team collected the common claims : most teams sit between 5 and 15 per cent, some as low as 2 per cent, and about 40 per cent after much effort. The same team made an important point in a companion piece . They could not find a single rigorous study that validates these "typical" percentages.
We agree with that caution, and it does not change the conclusion. You do not need a precise industry benchmark to act. Even if your real figure were three times higher than the commonly quoted range, most of each case's life would still be spent waiting. The question worth answering is not "what is normal?" It is "where does our work wait, and why?"
Little's Law: why open work equals slow work
In 1961 John Little published a proof of the queuing formula L = λW . It is now known as Little's Law. In plain terms: the average number of items in a system equals the average arrival rate multiplied by the average time each item spends in the system. Little later reflected on its practical reach in a 50th-anniversary paper.
Rearranged, it says something every operations leader should keep in mind:
Average time per case = work in progress ÷ throughput
Illustrative example: a team completes 40 matters a week and has 200 open. The average matter takes about five weeks. If the same team, doing the same work at the same pace, holds 100 matters open instead of 200, the average falls to about two and a half weeks.
The law describes long-run averages in a reasonably stable system, so treat it as a guide rather than a stopwatch. But the direction is reliable. Starting more work than you finish does not make you faster. It makes every case slower, because each one spends longer queued behind the others.
Why "everyone at full utilisation" backfires
Professional services firms are built around utilisation: billable hours, chargeable time, capacity plans that aim to keep everyone busy. That makes sense for cost. It is damaging for flow.
Queuing theory has shown for decades that waiting time does not rise in a straight line as utilisation rises. It climbs slowly at first, then very sharply as resources approach full capacity, and more so when work arrives unevenly. Kingman's formula is the standard approximation. In a services team the arrivals are client requests, and the variability is everything that makes services work hard to predict. A team planned to run at 95 per cent will have long queues almost by design.
Don Reinertsen made this argument for product development in The Principles of Product Development Flow . His point applies directly to services. In knowledge work, inventory is information. It is invisible, so queues go unmanaged. You cannot walk the floor and see half-finished matters stacked against a wall. They sit in inboxes and systems, and the only symptom is that everything takes longer than it should.
Where waiting hides in services work
When teams first measure flow, the waiting usually clusters in a few familiar places:
Approvals. A review or sign-off step owned by one senior person who is, quite reasonably, busy with other things.
Specialist queues. Work that only one team or person can do, such as compliance, tax or conflicts checks, and that everyone else is waiting on.
Waiting on the client. Missing documents and unanswered questions. Some of this is outside your control. More of it than you expect is caused by asking for things late or one at a time.
Batching. Work that is held until "we do those on Thursdays", so a case finished on Friday waits six days for the next batch.
Hand-offs between systems. Information re-keyed from email into a practice system, or from a CRM into billing, whenever someone gets to it.
Separating internal waiting from client waiting matters. It stops a team blaming clients for delays it created, and it shows which delays are worth automating.
How to measure your own flow efficiency
Pick one workflow with a clear start and finish that clients or revenue depend on: onboarding, new matters, claims, monthly close.
Define its states as they exist in your systems: created, assigned, in progress, waiting on client, in review, complete.
Pull timestamps for a few hundred recent cases from the systems where those state changes are recorded.
Classify time as active or waiting. Start with system states. They will be imperfect. That is fine for a first pass, as long as you are consistent.
Find the biggest queue, not the slowest step. The step with the most work waiting in front of it is usually the constraint on the whole flow.
Then resist the instinct to speed up the work at that step. First ask why work waits there, and whether you can start less, batch less or remove the hand-off. Making people faster is hard. Making work wait less is usually much easier, and it moves the number clients actually experience.
Questions
What is flow efficiency?
Flow efficiency is the percentage of a work item's total elapsed time during which someone is actively working on it. If a case takes ten working days end to end but receives one working day of actual effort, its flow efficiency is 10 per cent.
What is a good flow efficiency for knowledge work?
There is no rigorously validated benchmark. Practitioners often cite 5 to 15 per cent as typical and around 40 per cent as very good. It is more useful to track your own figure over time and find where your work waits than to chase an external number.
How does Little's Law apply to services businesses?
Little's Law says average time in a system equals work in progress divided by throughput. For a services team, holding fewer cases open at once, without changing how fast cases are worked, lowers the average time each case takes.
Sources
Little, J. D. C. (1961). A proof for the queuing formula: L = λW. Operations Research.
Little, J. D. C. (2011). Little's Law as viewed on its 50th anniversary. Operations Research.
ASOS Tech, Uncovering the real numbers behind flow efficiency
ASOS Tech, The many flaws of flow efficiency
Scrum.org, Business efficiency: watch the ball, not the player
Kingman's formula (queueing theory)
Reinertsen, D. G. (2009). The Principles of Product Development Flow.

## Why automation programs stall, and how to choose your first five
URL: https://missioncntrl.io/news/why-automation-programs-stall
Published: 2026-11-22

Key points
EY has reported that 30 to 50 per cent of initial RPA projects fail. MIT's 2025 research found most generative AI pilots produce no measurable P&L impact. The pattern repeats with each wave of technology.
The common cause is not the technology. It is choosing what to automate by intuition and visibility rather than by measured flow.
Automating a step that is not the bottleneck saves effort but rarely makes the business faster. It can simply grow the queue in front of the real constraint.
Choose your first automations on five tests: volume, wait time removed, rule stability, data availability and position relative to the bottleneck.
Automation has a striking record of over-promising in the pilot and under-delivering at scale. In robotic process automation, EY reported in its Get ready for robots paper that it had seen as many as 30 to 50 per cent of initial RPA projects fail. It was explicit that this was not a reflection of the technology. Among the common issues it listed were treating RPA as IT-led rather than business-led, and postponing the business case until after proofs of concept.
Generative AI is repeating the pattern faster. MIT NANDA's 2025 report The GenAI Divide found that 95 per cent of organisations in its research had seen no measurable return from generative AI. Only 5 per cent of custom enterprise AI tools reached production. The headline figure deserves caution. It comes from a preliminary study based on interviews, surveys and a sample of deployments, not a census. But the authors' explanation will be familiar to anyone who lived through RPA. Coverage of the report summarises it as brittle workflows, weak contextual learning and misalignment with day-to-day operations. The report also noted that the biggest returns appeared in back-office operations, not in the sales and marketing tools that attract most budget.
Meanwhile the theoretical ceiling keeps rising. McKinsey estimated in 2023 that current generative AI and other technologies have the potential to automate work activities that absorb 60 to 70 per cent of employees' time . The gap between that potential and what organisations actually bank is the real story. It is mostly a selection problem.
The real reason programs stall: they automate what they can see
Most automation backlogs are built the same way. A workshop is run. Teams nominate tasks that are repetitive and annoying. A consultant scores them on effort and feasibility. The quick wins are built first.
The flaw is in the input. Teams nominate the steps they personally perform and can describe: re-keying a form, renaming files, sending a reminder. They cannot nominate the delays between steps, because those delays belong to no one. Deloitte's intelligent automation research is telling here. Process fragmentation was cited by 36 per cent of respondents as the main barrier to adoption, more than twice the share citing IT readiness.
So programs fill up with automations of visible tasks inside single teams. Each one saves real effort. Then the business case is reviewed a year later. Clients are not served any faster, headcount has not changed, and the finance team cannot find the savings. The program loses sponsorship and stalls.
Why saving effort is not the same as moving faster
Eliyahu Goldratt's theory of constraints makes a simple point. The throughput of a whole process is limited by its tightest constraint. Improving any step other than the constraint does not increase throughput.
In automation terms, imagine an onboarding flow where documents are collected, checked, approved by a partner and then set up in the billing system. The partner approval is the constraint: work queues there for days. Automate document checking and it becomes faster, but nothing reaches the partner sooner in any way that matters. Checked files simply join a longer queue. The flow is no quicker and the saving is hard to bank.
Now automate the transfer from approval into billing, and pre-assemble everything the partner needs so approval takes minutes rather than a search. Elapsed time drops, cash arrives sooner and the benefit is visible to the client. The second automation might save fewer hours on paper. It is worth far more.
This is why we argue that the right unit for selecting automation is the flow , not the task. You need to know where work waits before you decide what to build.
How to choose your first five
Before anything is built, every candidate should be measured against the same five tests. Ideally this uses data from your own systems rather than estimates from a workshop.
Volume. How many times a month does this happen? Automation rewards repetition. A painful task that happens twice a month rarely pays back.
Wait time removed. Does automating this shorten elapsed time for the case, or only effort for the person? Prefer candidates at or immediately around the bottleneck, and at hand-offs between teams or systems.
Rule stability. How many variants does the step have in practice? If cases take a dozen different paths, automate the dominant path first and route the rest to people. Do not try to encode every exception on day one.
Data availability. Is the information the automation needs already captured in a system, in a consistent format? If not, the first project is data capture, not automation.
Ownership. Is there a named person who owns the outcome and will maintain the automation? EY and UiPath both point to programs that underestimate the work required after go-live . An automation without an owner decays as soon as the process around it changes.
Score each candidate. Size the value in hours and in elapsed time (we cover how to do this credibly in a separate guide ). Then pick five that sit on the constrained path. A good first portfolio usually includes one or two hand-off automations, one data-capture fix and one or two classic task automations, chosen because they feed the bottleneck rather than because they were nominated loudest.
Set kill criteria before you start
The other habit that separates programs that scale from those that stall is deciding in advance what failure looks like. Before building, write down three things: the measure the automation should move (elapsed time, hours, error rate), the expected size of the change, and the date by which you will check. If it does not move, switch it off and redeploy the effort.
That sounds obvious. In practice almost nobody does it, which is why automation estates fill up with bots and workflows that nobody can quite justify and nobody wants to turn off. Building fewer things and measuring them properly is less exciting than a long backlog. It is also how the 5 per cent get ahead.
Questions
Why do so many automation projects fail?
The most common reasons are choosing the wrong processes, treating automation as an IT project rather than a business one, and building before there is a business case. EY has reported that 30 to 50 per cent of initial RPA projects fail. It attributes this to how projects are run, not to the technology.
How should you choose which processes to automate first?
Test each candidate on volume, the wait time it removes, how stable its rules are, whether the data it needs is available and who will own it. Prioritise candidates on or around the process bottleneck and at hand-offs, because those shorten elapsed time as well as effort.
What is the difference between saving effort and improving flow?
Saving effort reduces the hours a person spends on a step. Improving flow reduces the elapsed time a case takes from start to finish. An automation can save effort without improving flow if the step it speeds up was never where work waited.
Sources
EY, Get ready for robots: why planning makes the difference between success and disappointment
The Register, coverage of MIT NANDA, The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025
Campus Technology, MIT report: most organisations see no business return on gen AI investments
McKinsey, The economic potential of generative AI (2023)
Deloitte, Automation with intelligence
Theory of constraints overview
UiPath, Why some RPA deployments fail

## How to build an automation business case your CFO will sign
URL: https://missioncntrl.io/news/automation-business-case-cfo
Published: 2026-11-22

Key points
Most automation business cases fail scrutiny for the same reasons. They treat hours saved as cash saved, ignore adoption ramps and running costs, and use estimated volumes rather than measured ones.
Build the case on measured volume and handling time, apply an automation rate and an adoption curve, then risk-adjust. Forrester's TEI method uses the same four elements: benefits, costs, flexibility and risk.
Keep two numbers separate: capacity released and cash realised. Capacity only becomes cash when it avoids a hire, removes contractor or overtime spend, or lets you grow without adding headcount.
Value elapsed time explicitly. Faster cycle times often matter more to cash flow and client experience than the hours saved.
Few documents lose credibility faster than an automation business case that promises to save "12 FTE". The CFO asks which 12 people, and when they are leaving. The answer is usually that nobody is leaving, and the case is quietly filed. That is a shame, because the underlying opportunity is often real. The problem is that it was sized in a way finance cannot bank.
This guide sets out a structure we think holds up in front of a sceptical finance team. It borrows from established investment appraisal practice. It is built on measured data rather than workshop estimates, and it is honest about the difference between time and money.
Five mistakes that sink automation business cases
Hours saved presented as cash. Releasing 2,000 hours across a team of 40 does not reduce cost unless something else changes. Without a plan for that capacity, the saving is theoretical.
Estimated volumes. "We do about 100 a week" is often wrong by a wide margin in either direction. Volumes should come from system records.
No adoption ramp. Automations rarely reach full use on day one. People keep doing things the old way, edge cases are routed back to humans, and trust is built slowly.
Missing running costs. Licences, hosting, monitoring and, above all, maintenance when the surrounding process or software changes. EY lists not having a business case before proofs of concept among the common causes of failed RPA projects. UiPath notes that companies underestimate the work required after automation is established .
Ignoring elapsed time. A case built only on effort misses what is often the bigger prize: work that finishes days sooner, so invoices go out sooner and clients notice.
A structure finance will recognise
Forrester's Total Economic Impact methodology has been used for over two decades to justify technology investments. It evaluates four components: cost, benefits, flexibility and risk. Its published studies present benefits and costs as risk-adjusted present values over three years. You do not need to commission a study to borrow the discipline. Every automation case should state each of those four elements explicitly.
1. Benefits: start from measured flow
Annual capacity released = cases per year × minutes per case removed × automation rate × adoption
Cases per year and current handling time should come from your systems. The automation rate is the share of cases the automation can handle without a person. Adoption is the share of eligible cases that actually go through it.
Convert hours to dollars with a fully loaded cost per productive hour, not a salary divided by 2,080. In Australia, average weekly ordinary time earnings for full-time adults were $2,083.70 in May 2026 , about $108,000 a year. Add the 12 per cent super guarantee that applies from 1 July 2025 , plus your own payroll tax, insurance, leave and overheads. Then divide by productive hours after leave and non-chargeable time. For an average full-time employee this often lands somewhere around $75 to $90 per productive hour. Use your own payroll data, by role, for the people whose work is affected.
2. Elapsed-time benefits: value the waiting
Where an automation removes a delay, size that separately. Two approaches work well:
Cash timing. If billing starts when onboarding completes, cutting onboarding from eight days to three brings five days of revenue forward on every new engagement. That is a working capital gain your CFO can calculate.
Cost of delay. Don Reinertsen argues that if you measure only one thing in flow, it should be cost of delay : what each day of waiting costs in lost revenue, penalties or client churn. Even a rough figure beats leaving it out.
3. Costs: include the whole life
Include build or implementation, licences and hosting, monitoring, and a realistic maintenance allowance for each year after go-live. Include the internal time of the people who test, train and own it. If you would not run the automation without an owner, the owner's time is a cost.
4. Risk and flexibility: adjust, do not inflate
Apply an explicit risk adjustment to benefits, for example a 10 to 25 per cent reduction depending on how well understood the process is, and state why. List flexibility value separately, such as the option to extend the automation to a second team, but do not add it to the headline. Finance teams trust cases that visibly discount their own optimism.
A worked example (illustrative)
The figures below are invented to show the method. They are not results from a client.
Process: client onboarding, 1,200 cases a month (14,400 a year), measured from system records.
Step automated: re-keying client details from intake forms into the practice and billing systems, measured at 35 minutes a case.
Automation rate: 70 per cent of cases handled end to end, the rest routed to a person.
Adoption: 50 per cent in the first quarter, 80 per cent after that.
Loaded cost: $80 per productive hour.
Steady-state capacity released: 14,400 × 35 min × 70% × 80% ≈ 4,704 hours a year, worth $376,320. Year one, with the ramp, is about 4,263 hours, worth $341,040.
Risk adjustment: 20 per cent, giving $272,832 in year one and $301,056 in each of years two and three.
Costs: $60,000 to build, $2,500 a month to run and $9,000 a year in maintenance from year two. That is $90,000 in year one and $39,000 a year after.
Three-year view (undiscounted): about $875,000 of risk-adjusted capacity value against $168,000 of cost.
Now the honest part. 4,704 hours is roughly 2.7 full-time people at around 1,750 productive hours each. That capacity becomes cash only if the business does something with it. Examples: absorbing growth without the next two hires, ending a contractor arrangement, or cutting overtime in peak periods. A credible case states which of those will happen, who has agreed to it and when. Anything not tied to a decision should be presented as capacity, not savings.
Then add the elapsed-time benefit separately. If removing re-keying also shortens onboarding by two days, and billing starts at the end of onboarding, two days of revenue on every new engagement is brought forward. The CFO can value that directly.
What makes a case believable
Measured inputs. Volumes, handling times and wait times from system data, with the date range stated.
Two headline numbers, clearly labelled: capacity released and cash realised.
Named decisions that turn capacity into cash, with owners.
A stated risk adjustment and the reasoning behind it.
A review date and the measure you will check, so the case can be proven right or wrong.
That last point matters most. A business case is a prediction. Cases that say in advance how they will be judged get approved more often. They also build the credibility that makes the next one easier.
Questions
How do you calculate the ROI of an automation?
Multiply measured annual volume by the minutes the automation removes per case, the share of cases it can handle and the expected adoption. Convert the hours to dollars at a fully loaded cost per productive hour, then apply a risk adjustment. Compare the result with the full-life cost of building, running and maintaining the automation over three years.
Are hours saved the same as money saved?
No. Hours saved are capacity released. They become money saved only when the business acts on them, for example by avoiding a hire, ending contractor or overtime spend, or growing without adding headcount. A credible business case reports the two separately.
What costs are usually missing from automation business cases?
Ongoing maintenance when processes or systems change, monitoring, licences and hosting, and the internal time of the people who test, train and own the automation. Adoption ramps are also often ignored, which overstates first-year benefits.
Sources
Forrester, Total Economic Impact methodology
Australian Bureau of Statistics, Average weekly earnings, May 2026
Australian Taxation Office, The final SG rate increase is coming on 1 July
EY, Get ready for robots
UiPath, Why some RPA deployments fail
PMI Disciplined Agile, Why looking at the value stream is so important

## How to map work without monitoring people
URL: https://missioncntrl.io/news/map-work-without-monitoring-people
Published: 2026-11-22

Key points
Process discovery (studying how work items move) and employee monitoring (studying what individuals do) are different activities. They carry different legal and cultural risks.
In Australia, NSW and the ACT require 14 days' written notice before computer surveillance. The ACT also requires consultation. Victoria's government has backed workplace surveillance reform in principle. Federal tranche 2 privacy reforms leave the employee records exemption in place.
In the UK, the ICO's 2023 guidance expects transparency, a clear purpose, the least intrusive means and usually a data protection impact assessment.
In the US, New York requires notice and acknowledgement for electronic monitoring. California's privacy law has covered employee data since 2023.
The safest and most useful design measures the work, not the worker: case-level metadata, aggregated views, no content capture and no individual scoring.
Any serious attempt to understand how work moves through an organisation runs into the same question from HR, legal and staff: is this surveillance? It is the right question to ask. The answer depends less on the technology than on what is measured, why and who can see it.
This article sets out the legal landscape in Australia, the UK and the US as we understand it in November 2026. It then argues for a design approach that makes the question easy to answer. It is general information, not legal advice. Workplace privacy law varies by jurisdiction and changes often, so take advice for your own situation.
Two very different things
Employee monitoring is about the individual: keystrokes, screenshots, active-window tracking, idle time, productivity scores. Its natural output is a judgement about a person.
Process discovery is about the work item: when a case was created, assigned, updated, waiting and closed, and which team handled each step. Academic process mining is built on exactly this. An event log records a case identifier, an activity and a timestamp . Its natural output is a picture of a workflow.
The two can blur. Case data still contains who did what, and a poorly designed tool can turn a process view into a league table of individuals. That is why design choices matter as much as legal compliance.
Australia
Federal privacy law. The Privacy Act 1988 contains an employee records exemption for private-sector employers. It covers acts directly related to a current or former employment relationship and the employee records the employer holds. Do not read that as a free pass. A new statutory tort for serious invasions of privacy commenced on 10 June 2025 , and commentators note it may limit how far employers can rely on the exemption. The exemption also does not cover contractors, clients or other third parties whose information appears in workflow data. Reform of the exemption was recommended by the Privacy Act Review. But the tranche 2 exposure draft released on 31 August 2026 does not address it.
New South Wales. The Workplace Surveillance Act 2005 regulates camera, computer and tracking surveillance of employees at work. Notice must be given at least 14 days before surveillance begins, unless the employee agrees to less. Computer surveillance must also be carried out in line with a policy the employee has been told about.
Australian Capital Territory. The Workplace Privacy Act 2011 also requires 14 days' written notice for optical, tracking and data surveillance. It adds a duty to consult in good faith with workers who raise concerns during that period.
Victoria. A Legislative Assembly committee tabled its Inquiry into workplace surveillance report on 13 May 2025 with 18 recommendations. They include new technology-neutral laws requiring surveillance to be reasonable, necessary and proportionate. The government's November 2025 response gave in-principle support to 15 of the 18 recommendations . Organisations with Victorian staff should expect stricter rules.
United Kingdom
On 3 October 2023 the Information Commissioner's Office published guidance on monitoring workers under the UK GDPR. Summaries from Simmons & Simmons and Hunton draw out the essentials:
Tell workers about the nature, extent and reasons for monitoring.
Do not monitor "just in case". Document why you are monitoring and what you will do with the information.
Use the least intrusive means that achieves the purpose.
Carry out a data protection impact assessment where processing is likely to be high risk. The ICO encourages one even where it is not strictly required.
Recognise that people working from home have a greater expectation of privacy.
United States
There is no single federal standard for workplace monitoring, so state law matters.
New York. Since 7 May 2022, Civil Rights Law § 52-c has required private employers that monitor employees' telephone, email or internet use to give written notice on hiring, obtain an acknowledgement and post a notice. Civil penalties start at $500 for a first violation. Connecticut and Delaware have similar notice laws.
California. The employee data exemption in the California Consumer Privacy Act expired on 1 January 2023 . Covered employers now owe California staff privacy notices, access and deletion rights, and appropriate contracts with service providers.
Our view: measure the work, not the worker
Across these regimes the direction is consistent. Regulators want transparency, a clear purpose, proportionality and minimal data. A process discovery program designed around those principles is easier to defend, easier to roll out and more useful. People cooperate with a project they understand, and resist one they suspect.
We think seven design principles matter most:
Case-level, not person-level. The unit of analysis is the work item and its journey. Views are by workflow, step and team.
Metadata, not content. Timestamps, status changes and assignments are enough to show where work waits. The contents of emails, documents and messages are not needed and should not be collected.
Aggregate by default. Report at team or step level with minimum group sizes, so individuals cannot be singled out.
No individual performance scoring. Process data should never become a ranking of people. If it does, trust and data quality both collapse.
A written purpose. State what the program is for, such as reducing cycle time or sizing automation, and what it will not be used for.
Notice and consultation everywhere, including where the law does not strictly require them. Tell people before anything starts, explain what is and is not collected, and give them a channel for concerns.
Short retention and tight access. Keep data only as long as the analysis needs it, and limit who can see raw records.
These principles also produce better analysis. Systems record wait time between steps faithfully. Watching people in the moment mostly shows who looks busy. The question that matters to a services business is where the work waits. You can answer it fully without looking at anyone's screen.
Questions
Is process mining the same as employee monitoring?
No. Process mining analyses how work items move through a workflow using system event data such as case identifiers, activities and timestamps. Employee monitoring tracks what individuals do, such as keystrokes, screenshots or active time. Process discovery can still involve personal information, so it should be designed and disclosed carefully.
Do Australian employers need to give notice before computer surveillance?
In New South Wales and the Australian Capital Territory, yes. Both require written notice at least 14 days before surveillance begins, unless the employee agrees to less. The ACT also requires good-faith consultation. Other states regulate surveillance differently, and Victoria is moving towards new laws. Take legal advice for your situation.
What does the UK ICO expect from employers that monitor workers?
The ICO's October 2023 guidance expects employers to tell workers what monitoring takes place and why, to avoid monitoring "just in case", to use the least intrusive means available and to carry out a data protection impact assessment where the processing is likely to be high risk.
